title_en: China Construction Bank, Pudong Branch v. Zhongji Company, et al. — dispute over loan contract
keywords_en: Civil; loan contract dispute; second instance; Supreme People's Court; Shanghai; Beijing; legal person; financial institution; General Principles of Civil Law; Economic Contract Law; Guarantee Law; authenticity of seal on guarantee contract; genuine expression of guarantee intent; determination of validity of altered seal; appellate reversal; loan contract; guarantee letter; seal alteration; foreign currency loan; genuine expression of intent; contract dispute; loan contract dispute against Zhongji Company et al.
full_text_en:
CCB Pudong Branch v.  
China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation, et al. — dispute over loan contract  

[Ruling Summary]  

Where a judicial appraisal of a disputed contract text determines that the signature of one party is forged and its seal is altered, and neither the evidence submitted by the parties nor the court's investigation can prove that the altered seal was affixed by that party itself or at its instruction, nor can it prove that the party was aware of the existence of the disputed contract text and failed to deny it, or used the altered seal in other business activities, or was aware of another's use of the altered seal and failed to deny it, then the disputed contract text cannot be determined or presumed to represent the true intention of that party.  

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court  
(2001) Min Er Zhong Zi No. 155  

Appellant (defendant at first instance): China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation. Domicile: Building 16-17, Zone 3, Fangzhuang Fangxingyuan, Fengtai District, Beijing.  
Legal Representative: Xue Zhao, Chairman of the Board.  
Agent ad litem: Zhao Zihe, employee of the company.  
Agent ad litem: Pan Xiuping, attorney at Beijing Haituo Law Firm.  

Respondent (plaintiff at first instance): China Construction Bank, Shanghai Pudong Branch. Domicile: No. 201, Yincheng East Road, Pudong New Area, Shanghai.  
Responsible Person: Xie Ping, President of the Branch.  
Agent ad litem: Huang Xiang, employee of the Branch.  
Agent ad litem: Ye Hangsheng, attorney at Shanghai Guangting Law Firm.  

Respondent (defendant at first instance): Shanghai Zhongyi International Trade Development Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 120, Laoshan West Road, Pudong, Shanghai.  
Legal Representative: Wang Tianjue, General Manager of the company.  
Agent ad litem: Guan Xiaowei, employee of Zhongyi International Group Co., Ltd.  
Agent ad litem: Han Fangsheng, employee of Zhongyi International Group Co., Ltd.  

The appellant, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation (hereinafter "Zhongji Company"), dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2001) Hu Gao Jing Zhong Zi No. 2 rendered by the Shanghai High People's Court in the dispute over a loan contract with the respondents, China Construction Bank, Shanghai Pudong Branch (hereinafter "CCB Pudong Branch") and Shanghai Zhongyi International Trade Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Shanghai Zhongyi Company"), appealed to this Court. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law, with presiding judge Jiang Wei, and acting judges Qian Xiaochen and Yang Zhengyu, to hear the case. The court clerk was Zhang Ruihua. The case is now concluded.  

The court of first instance found the following facts:  
1. On August 19, 1996, CCB Pudong Branch and Shanghai Zhongyi Company entered into a foreign exchange loan contract. It stipulated that CCB Pudong Branch would provide a working capital loan of USD 4.5 million to Shanghai Zhongyi Company; the loan term was from August 19, 1996, to August 18, 1997; the annual loan interest rate was the one-year foreign exchange working capital loan rate of China Construction Bank, floating every six months; interest payment dates were March 20, June 20, September 20, and December 20 of each year; if Shanghai Zhongyi Company failed to repay any amount due under the contract on time, CCB Pudong Branch would charge overdue interest on the overdue amount from the due date until the date of actual payment, at a rate of 1.3 times the loan interest rate (the rate at the time of default). On the same day, CCB Pudong Branch transferred USD 4.5 million into Shanghai Zhongyi Company's account as agreed. Thereafter, Shanghai Zhongyi Company paid interest to CCB Pudong Branch from the loan date to December 23, 1996, and additionally paid USD 120,000 in interest on January 25, 1998, but the remaining amount has been in arrears. As of January 20, 1998, Shanghai Zhongyi Company still owed CCB Pudong Branch principal of USD 4.5 million and interest (including interest within the term and overdue interest) of USD 307,330.08.  
2. Zhongji Company issued an Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee to CCB Pudong Branch for the loan in dispute. The letter stated that the guaranteed amount was USD 4.5 million, plus interest and related expenses incurred under the loan; Zhongji Company guaranteed to repay all or part of the overdue principal, interest, and related expenses that Shanghai Zhongyi Company failed to repay under the loan contract, and guaranteed to repay the overdue principal, interest, and expenses of Shanghai Zhongyi Company within 14 days after receiving written notice from CCB Pudong Branch; the guarantee was a continuing guarantee and indemnity, effective from the date of signing until the guaranteed amount was fully repaid by Shanghai Zhongyi Company or Zhongji Company. The letter bore the signature and seal of Xue Zhao and the official seal of Zhongji Company.  
3. The official seal of Zhongji Company affixed on the above guarantee did not match the seal specimen filed by Zhongji Company with the State Administration for Industry and Commerce.  
4. Shanghai Zhongyi Company was jointly invested and established in 1995 by Zhongji Company and a third party, Zhongyi International Economic Group Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Zhongyi Group"). When handling the registration of Shanghai Zhongyi Company, Zhongji Company, as one of the investing shareholders, used the disputed guarantee seal on multiple documents submitted to the Pudong New Area Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter "Pudong AIC") for establishment registration. Additionally, Zhongji Company also used the disputed guarantee seal in two packing loan transactions with ING Bank Shanghai Branch (hereinafter "ING Bank").  

To recover the debt, CCB Pudong Branch filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai High People's Court on February 28, 1998, requesting Shanghai Zhongyi Company to repay all loan principal and interest, and requesting Zhongji Company to bear joint and several guarantee liability for the above debt based on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee. After accepting the case, the Shanghai High People's Court rendered a civil judgment (1998) Hu Gao Jing Chu Zi No. 10 on March 10, 1999, ordering Shanghai Zhongyi Company to repay CCB Pudong Branch the principal and interest of USD 4.5 million, and Zhongji Company to bear joint and several liability for clearing the debt. Dissatisfied with this judgment, Zhongji Company appealed to this Court. After accepting the appeal, this Court issued a civil ruling (1999) Jing Zhong Zi No. 179 on February 3, 2001, holding that the first-instance judgment had unclear facts and insufficient evidence, and remanded the case to the Shanghai High People's Court for retrial.  

After retrial, the Shanghai High People's Court held that this case was a dispute over a loan contract, the foreign exchange loan contract between CCB Pudong Branch and Shanghai Zhongyi Company was valid and binding on both parties, and both should perform their obligations accordingly. After CCB Pudong Branch disbursed the loan as agreed, Shanghai Zhongyi Company failed to repay principal and interest on time, which was a clear breach of contract and should bear corresponding civil liability. Shanghai Zhongyi Company's defense requesting a reduction of its liability for the loan interest lacked legal basis and was not supported. Although the seal affixed on the guarantee in dispute did not match the seal specimen filed by Zhongji Company with the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, Zhongji Company had used the same seal multiple times in other business activities, so it should be deemed that Zhongji Company approved the seal, and providing the guarantee for the loan in dispute was Zhongji Company's true intention. As the guarantor for the loan in dispute, Zhongji Company should also bear corresponding guarantee liability as agreed. Since the guarantee in dispute did not clearly specify the type of guarantee, Zhongji Company should bear joint and several guarantee liability. After bearing the guarantee liability, Zhongji Company was entitled to seek recourse from Shanghai Zhongyi Company according to law. Shanghai Zhongyi Company's defense that it had never asked Zhongji Company to provide a guarantee for the loan, and the defense of Shanghai Zhongyi Company and Zhongji Company that the seal on the guarantee was affixed by Wu Xiaoping using an altered seal of Zhongji Company, lacked factual basis and were not accepted by the court. After deliberation by the judicial committee of the court, in accordance with Article 84 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC, Article 40, paragraph 2 of the Economic Contract Law of the PRC, and Articles 6, 18(2), 19, 21, and 31 of the Guarantee Law of the PRC, the court ruled: 1. Shanghai Zhongyi Company shall repay CCB Pudong Branch the loan principal of USD 4.5 million within 10 days of the judgment taking effect; 2. Shanghai Zhongyi Company shall repay CCB Pudong Branch the loan interest of USD 307,330.08 (calculated up to January 20, 1998) within 10 days of the judgment taking effect. Overdue interest incurred after January 20, 1998, shall be calculated according to the contract until full payment; 3. Zhongji Company shall bear joint and several liability for clearing the payment obligations in items 1 and 2 above. After bearing the corresponding guarantee liability, Zhongji Company is entitled to seek recourse from Shanghai Zhongyi Company. The case acceptance fee of RMB 209,021.45 shall be borne jointly by Shanghai Zhongyi Company and Zhongji Company.  

Dissatisfied with the above civil judgment of the Shanghai High People's Court, Zhongji Company appealed to this Court, claiming: 1. Zhongji Company had no knowledge of the loan guarantee; the seal of Zhongji Company on the guarantee provided by CCB Pudong Branch was a counterfeit, not representing Zhongji Company's true intention, and thus the company should not bear guarantee liability; 2. When CCB Pudong Branch disbursed the loan to Shanghai Zhongyi Company, it failed to conduct a verification of the guarantee as required by the relevant regulations of the People's Construction Bank of China, and thus had corresponding fault in the loan process; 3. The fact that the counterfeit seal appeared multiple times in this case could not be interpreted as Zhongji Company's approval of the counterfeit seal; 4. Wu Xiaoping's act of altering the seal to defraud bank loans constituted serious financial fraud, and the case should be transferred to the relevant judicial authorities for criminal investigation. It requested the court of second instance to amend the judgment and rule that Zhongji Company should not bear guarantee liability.  

CCB Pudong Branch argued in response: 1. Although the seal affixed on the guarantee in dispute did not match the seal specimen filed by Zhongji Company with the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, Zhongji Company had used the same seal multiple times in other business activities, and the loan that Zhongji Company applied for from ING Bank using the so-called counterfeit seal had been deposited into Zhongji Company's account at the Beijing Branch of the Agricultural Bank of China; Zhongji Company not only used this loan but also repaid it. Therefore, Zhongji Company approved the seal, and providing the guarantee for the loan in dispute was Zhongji Company's true intention; as guarantor, Zhongji Company should bear guarantee liability; 2. The handling officer of CCB Pudong Branch conducted a verification of the guarantee contract in dispute, and whether verification was conducted does not affect Zhongji Company's guarantee liability; 3. Zhongji Company had no evidence to prove that the seal on the guarantee was forged by Wu Xiaoping; this case was an economic dispute and did not need to be transferred to other judicial authorities for criminal investigation. It requested the rejection of Zhongji Company's appeal and the affirmation of the original judgment.  

This Court confirms the facts found by the first-instance judgment in items 1 and 3, the fact regarding the content of the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee in item 2, and the fact regarding the multiple uses of the disputed guarantee seal in item 4. However, the fact that the altered seal was used by Zhongji Company cannot be confirmed. The facts found by this Court are as follows: To support its claim that Zhongji Company should bear guarantee liability for the loan to Shanghai Zhongyi Company, CCB Pudong Branch submitted to the court of first instance an Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee, on page 3 of which, in the column for "legal representative," the name "Xue Zhao" was written, and in the column for "guarantor," a seal with the text "China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation" was affixed. At Zhongji Company's request, during the second instance, this Court commissioned the Ministry of Public Security of the PRC to conduct a judicial appraisal of the authenticity of the seal with the text "China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation" and the signature "Xue Zhao" on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee. The Ministry issued a Physical Evidence Appraisal Report (2002) Gong Wu Zheng Jian Zi No. 0331. The report stated: 1. The seal impression of "China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation" on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was formed by the same seal as the seal impression of "Trade Development Department, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation." 2. The signature "Xue Zhao" on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was not written by the same person who provided the signature of Xue Zhao, legal representative of Zhongji Company, taken in court. Based on this, it can be determined that the signature "Xue Zhao" on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was not the personal signature of Xue Zhao, legal representative of Zhongji Company, and the seal impression of "China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation" on the guarantee was formed by altering the seal of "Trade Development Department, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation" by covering the words "Trade Development Department." During the first instance, Jin Shiping and Yuan Jing, the handling officers of CCB Pudong Branch for the above loan business, had submitted a written statement to the court of first instance, stating: At the end of July or beginning of August 1996, accompanied by Wu Xiaoping, they went to Zhongji Company at approximately 5:30 p.m. The legal representative of Zhongji Company had already left. The office director of the company, Zhang Zhizhong, received them and affixed the seal on the loan contract in their presence, stating that he would have the contract brought to Xue Zhao for signing in the evening. During the open court session of the first instance on November 18, 1998, Zhongji Company denied the above statements and requested Jin Shiping and Yuan Jing to identify Zhang Zhizhong in court. Jin Shiping and Yuan Jing both said that too much time had passed and they could not recognize him.  

It was further found that on January 19, 1994, Zhongji Company and Zhongmao International Enterprise Group Co., Ltd. (later changed to Zhongyi Group) entered into an Agreement on Cooperative Management of Import and Export Trade, stipulating that Zhongji Company would establish the Trade Development Department (hereinafter "Zhongji Company TD Department") and entrust it to Zhongyi Group for contracting operation; Zhongyi Group would be responsible for all business activities conducted by Zhongji Company TD Department and its personnel; all commercial risks, claims, and debts arising from the business activities of Zhongji Company TD Department would be borne by Zhongyi Group itself. The seal of Zhongji Company TD Department would be strictly controlled and used by Zhongyi Group. On January 24, 1994, Zhongji Company issued a Notice on the Establishment of the Import and Export Department and Trade Development Department of China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation, stating that the board meeting of Zhongji Company had decided to establish Zhongji Company TD Department, and the department would operate independently, with separate accounting and self-financing. Matters such as engraving seals and opening accounts would be handled by Zhongji Company TD Department in coordination with relevant departments. On April 5, 2001, Zhang Lijun, Chairman of Zhongyi Group, stated to the Haidian District Procuratorate of Beijing that after Zhongji Company TD Department was established, it was operated by Zhongyi Group, and Zhang Lijun concurrently served as General Manager of Zhongji Company TD Department. The seal "Trade Development Department, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation" engraved by Zhongji Company TD Department was kept and used by Zhongji Company TD Department. On March 3, 2002, Zhongyi Group submitted a written explanation to this Court, stating that since 1994, it had contracted to operate Zhongji Company TD Department, and the seal of Zhongji Company TD Department was used by Zhongyi Group from 1994 to 1997. In addition, the seal filing records of Zhongji Company also showed that the seal of Zhongji Company TD Department was not handed over to Zhongji Company's office until March 7, 1997.  

It was further found that on December 19, 1995, Zhongji Company TD Department applied to ING Bank for a packing loan totaling USD 710,990. In the applicant column, the seal "Financial Seal of Trade Development Department, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation" and the personal seal of Zhang Lijun were affixed. However, in the declaration column of the packing loan application documents (the main content was that the affixture agreed that the bank could, without prior notice, offset the funds in the sealed account against the affixture's liabilities to the bank), an altered Zhongji Company seal was affixed. On December 22, 1995, ING Bank remitted USD 710,990 to the Beijing Branch of the Agricultural Bank of China (hereinafter "ABC Beijing Branch"), and the funds were ultimately transferred into account No. 14801103019, which had been opened at Qingnianhu Sub-branch under ABC Beijing Branch. During the second instance, this Court inquired with ABC Beijing Branch and found that the account opening documents included three copies of the Account Opening Application, three copies of the Specimen Seal Card, and one copy of the business license of Zhongji Company as a legal person enterprise. On the account opening application and specimen seal card, the account holder was listed as "Trade Development Department, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation," the address as "Building 30, Jing'anli, Chaoyang District," and the column for review opinion of the superior department was left blank. The seal affixed on the specimen seal card was "Financial Seal of Trade Development Department, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation." On the same day of receipt, Zhongji Company TD Department transferred the funds into the account of Zhongyi Group Company at the same sub-branch, and the seal affixed on the bank transfer voucher was the reserved "Financial Seal of Trade Development Department, China Export Commodities Base Construction Corporation."  

In October 1995, Zhongji Company and Zhongyi Group jointly applied to the Pudong New Area Administration for Industry and Commerce in Shanghai for the establishment of Shanghai Zhongyi Company, and jointly entrusted Chen Gongchen, an employee of Zhongyi Group, as agent to handle the registration matters. In the establishment registration documents of Shanghai Zhongyi Company at the Pudong New Area AIC, all documents submitted in the name of Zhongji Company, including the report on application for company establishment, shareholders' resolution, and articles of association, bore the altered Zhongji Company seal. During the open court session of the second instance, the agent of Zhongji Company stated in court that Zhongji Company agreed to and invested in the establishment of Shanghai Zhongyi Company, but was unaware that the agent handling the registration matters used the altered Zhongji Company seal. On February 4, 1997, Shanghai Zhongyi Company made a resolution at its first third shareholders' meeting, with the subject of Zhongji Company transferring all its 51% shares to Tianjin Zhongyi Shipping Company. On the shareholders' resolution and the application for equity transfer submitted by Zhongji Company and Zhongyi Group to the Pudong New Area AIC the following day, both bore Zhongji Company's seal, which matched the seal specimen filed with the State Administration for Industry and Commerce.  

Regarding the above facts of using the altered Zhongji Company seal, CCB Pudong Branch was not aware of them when it accepted the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee. It was only after the dispute arose that CCB Pudong Branch learned of the above facts through investigation and evidence collection.  

It was further found that on September 29, 1998, the Public Security Bureau of Changzhi City, Shanxi Province, arrested Wu Xiaoping on suspicion of fraud and misappropriation of huge sums of money, and included the USD 4.5 million in dispute in the scope of investigation into whether Wu Xiaoping's forgery of Zhongji Company's seal constituted fraud. On March 29, 2001, the Haidian District Procuratorate of Beijing also initiated an investigation into Wu Xiaoping's suspected crimes, which also included the loan in dispute. On January 28, 2000, the Changzhi City Public Security Bureau issued a detention warrant for Jin Shiping. Later, because Wu Xiaoping and Jin Shiping absconded, the above suspected criminal cases have not been confirmed. On March 15, 2000, the Changzhi City Public Security Bureau placed Wu Xiaoping on the national wanted list, and he has not yet been captured.

After receiving the US$4.5 million loan from CCB Pudong Branch, Shanghai Zhongyi Company only paid the interest from the date of borrowing to December 23, 1996 within the agreed repayment period. Thereafter, on January 25, 1998, it again repaid interest of US$120,000 to CCB Pudong Branch. As of January 20, 1998, Shanghai Zhongyi Company still owed CCB Pudong Branch principal of US$4.5 million and interest of US$307,330.08.

In the opinion of this Court, the foreign exchange loan contract entered into between CCB Pudong Branch and Shanghai Zhongyi Company does not violate legal provisions. The contract bears the official seals of both parties, and after CCB Pudong Branch delivered the funds to Shanghai Zhongyi Company in accordance with the contract, Shanghai Zhongyi Company used the entire amount and paid part of the interest to CCB Pudong Branch. Based on this, the loan contract should be confirmed as legally valid and effective. CCB Pudong Branch issued the loan to Shanghai Zhongyi Company in accordance with the contract and performed its contractual obligations. However, Shanghai Zhongyi Company failed to repay the loan principal and interest to CCB Pudong Branch as agreed, and shall bear corresponding civil liability according to law. The original judgment ordering Shanghai Zhongyi Company to repay the loan principal of US$4.5 million and corresponding interest to CCB Pudong Branch was not improper. Moreover, Shanghai Zhongyi Company did not appeal this portion of the judgment, and this Court shall uphold it according to law.

The focus of the dispute in this second instance is whether the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was established. Article 32 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Contract Law) provides: "Where the parties enter into a contract in written form, the contract is established when the parties sign or affix their seals thereto." This provision indicates that either the signature or the seal of a party can establish the contract.

The signature of a party includes the signature of the natural person himself or his authorized agent, or the signature of the legal representative or responsible person of a legal person enterprise or other economic organization, or his authorized agent. Article 38 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "The responsible person who, in accordance with the law or the provisions of the articles of association of the legal person, exercises the functions and powers on behalf of the legal person is its legal representative." Article 43 provides: "An enterprise legal person shall bear civil liability for the operational activities of its legal representative and other employees." A contract signed by the legal representative of an enterprise represents the expression of intent of the enterprise and can produce the legal effect of the establishment of the contract. The signature on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee in dispute in this case is that of the legal representative, and there is no act of an authorized agent. However, the signature of the legal representative, Xue Zhao, was forged by another person. Xue Zhao should not be held responsible for acts that were not signed by him, and it cannot be determined on this basis that the content of the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee reflected the intent of Zhongji Company. Therefore, a forged signature cannot cause the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee in dispute to be established and become effective, and Zhongji Company does not bear civil liability due to the forged signature of the legal representative.

Affixing a seal can also produce the effect of the establishment of a contract. The significance of affixing a seal on a contract is to prove that the content of the contract represents the expression of intent of the party recorded by the seal. At this time, the impression of the seal on the contract has an evidentiary function. For a contract affixed with a genuine seal, the rights and obligations thereof shall be borne by that party. The Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee in dispute in this case was affixed with a seal that was altered from the seal of the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company, and is not the official seal of Zhongji Company. The Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee does not necessarily represent the intent of Zhongji Company, nor does it represent the intent of the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company.

Whether Zhongji Company should bear guarantee liability based on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee requires a comprehensive determination based on the relevant facts of this case. If the act of affixing the altered seal was done by Zhongji Company itself, then even though the seal was altered, it can still represent the expression of intent of Zhongji Company, and Zhongji Company should bear guarantee liability. However, the seal of the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company was held by Zhongyi Group at the time the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was issued. Although the business handling personnel of CCB Pudong Branch claimed that the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was handed over to Zhang Zhizhong, the office director of Zhongji Company, for the company to affix its seal, during the first instance trial they could not identify Zhang Zhizhong. The fact that the altered seal on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was affixed by Zhongji Company could not be corroborated. Therefore, CCB Pudong Branch's claim that the altered seal on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee was affixed by Zhongji Company is unsupported by evidence.

In the absence of supporting evidence, the original judgment improperly determined that Zhongji Company had repeatedly used the altered seal of Zhongji Company in other business activities. The application by the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company to ABN AMRO Bank for a packing loan occurred during the period when the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company was under the operation and management of Zhongyi Group Company. This packing loan was applied for in the name of the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company. The account number 14801103019, into which the loan was subsequently remitted, was also opened upon the application of the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company, and the transfer voucher for the loan was also affixed with the financial seal of the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company. There is no evidence indicating a direct connection between the application and transfer process of this packing loan and Zhongji Company. Although the account opening documents for the aforementioned account 14801103019 included a copy of the business license of Zhongji Company as a legal person enterprise, since a copy of an enterprise's business license can be obtained from multiple channels such as the industrial and commercial authorities, tax authorities, and the enterprise itself, the mere fact that the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company held a copy of Zhongji Company's business license cannot establish that the copy was provided by Zhongji Company to the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company. Moreover, even if it were determined that the copy was provided by Zhongji Company, since the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company was independently operated and managed by Zhongyi Group Company at that time, it still could not be determined that Zhongji Company was aware of the establishment of account 14801103019 by the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company. Nor could it be determined that Zhongji Company was aware of the Trade Development Department of Zhongji Company's application for the US$710,990 packing loan from ING Bank Shanghai Branch. Even less could it be determined that Zhongji Company was aware of the use of the altered seal of Zhongji Company in the application documents for the aforementioned packing loan. Even if Zhongji Company knew that another person used an altered seal in a certain transaction and ratified that transaction, such ratification pertains only to the agency act of that other person in that transaction, and its effect is limited to that specific agency matter. When Zhongji Company transferred part of its equity in Shanghai Zhongyi Company, it used a legitimate seal. This act can be considered a ratification of the establishment of Shanghai Zhongyi Company. Without this act or other acts of ratification, the altered seal still cannot represent the intent of Zhongji Company. In the opening of the account at the Beijing Branch of the Agricultural Bank of China and the letter of credit transaction with ING Bank Shanghai Branch, there is no evidence that Zhongji Company knew of the use of the altered seal and ratified the aforementioned acts. Therefore, the repeated use of the altered seal of Zhongji Company by others does not produce the effect that the altered seal can represent the intent of Zhongji Company in every transaction. CCB Pudong Branch's argument that the loan applied for by Zhongji Company using the so-called fake seal from ING Bank Shanghai Branch was credited to Zhongji Company's account at the Beijing Branch of the Agricultural Bank of China, and that Zhongji Company not only used this loan but also repaid this loan, is inconsistent with the facts and is not accepted by this Court.

The reasons CCB Pudong Branch claims it believed the altered seal could represent Zhongji Company are, first, the process of affixing the seal, and second, the repeated use of the altered seal. As discussed above, CCB Pudong Branch cannot prove that the altered seal was affixed by Zhongji Company. The mere repeated use of the altered seal itself does not produce the effect of necessarily representing the expression of intent of Zhongji Company. Moreover, at the time CCB Pudong Branch accepted the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee, it did not know that the seal had been repeatedly used. It was only after the dispute arose that it gathered relevant evidence. It is evident that when CCB Pudong Branch accepted the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee, it did not rely on the repeated use of the seal as a reason to believe the seal could represent the expression of intent of Zhongji Company. As a professional financial institution, CCB Pudong Branch should have exercised a duty of care in conducting financial business. However, its handling personnel failed to perform their duties diligently by accepting a guarantee affixed with an altered seal. Zhongji Company has no fault in this matter and should not bear obligations under the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee.

In summary, judicial appraisal commissioned by this Court has confirmed that the signature of the legal representative of Zhongji Company on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee of CCB Pudong Branch was forged, and the official seal was formed by altering another official seal. Moreover, the evidence submitted by the parties and the investigation by this Court cannot prove that the altered seal of Zhongji Company was affixed by Zhongji Company itself or that it instructed another to affix it. It cannot be proven that Zhongji Company knew of the existence of the Letter of Guarantee without making a denial. It also cannot be proven that Zhongji Company itself used the altered seal of Zhongji Company in other business activities or that it knew another used the altered seal of Zhongji Company without making a denial. The signature and the altered seal of Zhongji Company on the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee cannot be determined or legally presumed to be the true expression of intent of Zhongji Company. Therefore, the Irrevocable Letter of Guarantee is not established, and Zhongji Company should not bear guarantee liability for the principal and interest of the US$4.5 million loan from Shanghai Zhongyi Company to CCB Pudong Branch. Zhongji Company's appeal that it should not bear guarantee liability in this case is well-founded, and this Court supports it according to law. The original judgment's determination that Shanghai Zhongyi Company should bear civil liability is clear in facts and correct in the application of law, and should be affirmed. However, the determination that Zhongji Company should bear joint and several guarantee liability is unclear in facts and erroneous in the application of law, and should be reversed.

Pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, items (1), (2), and (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court hereby renders the following judgment:

1. Affirm items 1 and 2 of the main text of the Civil Judgment (2001) Hu Gao Jing Chong Zi No. 2 of the Shanghai High People's Court;

2. Reverse item 3 of the main text of the Civil Judgment (2001) Hu Gao Jing Chong Zi No. 2 of the Shanghai High People's Court; and dismiss the litigation claim of China Construction Bank, Shanghai Pudong Branch, requesting China Export Base Development Corporation to bear guarantee liability.

Court acceptance fee for the first instance: RMB 209,021.45, to be borne by Shanghai Zhongyi International Trade Development Co., Ltd. Court acceptance fee for the second instance: RMB 209,021.45, to be borne by China Construction Bank, Shanghai Pudong Branch (the court acceptance fee for the second instance has been prepaid by China Export Base Development Corporation; this Court will not refund it, and China Construction Bank, Shanghai Pudong Branch shall directly pay the amount to China Export Base Development Corporation).

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge: Jiang Wei

Acting Judge: Qian Xiaochen

Acting Judge: Yang Zhengyu

Clerk: Zhang Ruihua

[Profile of the Presiding Judge]

Jiang Wei, Senior Judge: Born in 1959, holds a bachelor's degree in law, appointed Judge of the Supreme People's Court in 1994.
